workLog.phase: Build the corpus guard, then survive two reviews of it
actions: Implemented the corpus-comparability guard TDD. Wrote 18 tests first, confirmed 12 red, implemented an envelope format optimizer-results/1 carrying {schema, corpus, results}, and made gate refuse a pair whose corpora disagree. Reader accepts legacy bare mappings; the discriminator is a string-valued schema key, not the key alone, so a legacy file with a task named schema still parses as legacy.

Round 15 adversarial review with gpt-5.6-terra returned REJECT with three findings, all real. CRITICAL: the guard was reachable by deletion, since stripping the envelope off either side left two unknowns and unknowns compared. REQUIRED: an unvalidated corpus string reported a verified match, so two reports both carrying an empty fixture_set_sha compared as verified. REQUIRED: reading both results files in full before the ledger lock let a malformed verdict mapping answer in place of an exhausted budget.

Closed the CRITICAL with two changes rather than one. split now pins the corpus of the results it was drawn from, so the value lives in the baseline commitment and no results file can delete it. And one known corpus beside an unknown one now counts as a conflict, which covers splits drawn before the pin existed. Neither alone is sufficient.
Closed the first REQUIRED by validating the corpus form as 64 lowercase hex at both the extraction boundary and the envelope reader.

Closed the second REQUIRED by splitting the read. The pre-lock work is now a header-only read that answers unknown to every content problem and cannot raise, wrapped in the digest scrubber. The full read moved into _gate_decision, after the ledger guards and before the charge.

Argued one point down rather than absorbing it. The reviewer wanted the whole corpus check moved behind the ledger lock. It stayed ahead: the file's convention, visible in the out-of-range --max-p check and the split-drift refusal, is that structural-validity refusals precede ledger refusals, and an incomparable pair is unusable at any budget. The reviewer's real concern was the full read, which the header-only split fixes.
Rewrote the test that encoded the bypass. The old assertion said unknown beside known compares; it now says that pair is refused. Bending the code to a stale test would have re-opened the CRITICAL.
Re-proved against the real data after the redesign. Both the original incident pair and the same pair with the candidate envelope stripped now return REJECT, consultations 0, zero ledger files.

Stated the bound in the README and the ADR rather than leaving it to be found. The split is caller-supplied and its pin sits outside the fingerprint, so a caller who edits two files together can still push an incomparable pair through. This defends against omission, not an adversary.

Recorded defect shape 18 in the debate log: a refusal reachable by deletion is not a refusal, and the generalization that a guard with a cannot-determine state should be measured by what it costs to reach that state deliberately.

workLog.phase: Round 16 review: close five defects and correct a documented overclaim
actions: Second adversarial review of the corpus guard, gpt-5.6-terra, returned REJECT with five findings. Confirmed all five by running the code, not by reading it. Two CRITICAL, three REQUIRED.

CRITICAL 1, the documented property was wrong. README and ADR-087 both claimed the corpus refusal cannot be deleted. True of the results envelope, false of the split pin: deleting the split's corpus key leaves two agreeing results files and no disagreement to refuse. Did not take the reviewer's fix of requiring a pin before any ACCEPT, because a --tasks split pins nothing by construction and neither the rule nor the hook path publishes a corpus identity, so that rule would disable the gate for two of three artifact classes. Split the claim into two reported facts instead: corpus_verified for the two results agreeing, corpus_pinned for the split naming the corpus they carry.

CRITICAL 2, TOCTOU between the header preflight and the full read. The two reads were never reconciled, so the values the comparison scored from never had to match the values the guard checked. The conflict rule now runs again against the loaded ResultsFile values, before the consultation is charged. Both call sites now emit one shared refusal payload so they cannot drift.
REQUIRED 3, split corpus pin was unvalidated. A split carrying corpus of [] raised TypeError out of a set comprehension. Now validated with the same 64-lowercase-hex check the results files get.

REQUIRED 4, _corpus_header promised it could not raise on content and caught only ValueError. A JSON array nested 200000 deep raises RecursionError, which escaped as an uncaught traceback ahead of the ledger guard. Normalized in both _read_json and _corpus_header.

REQUIRED 5, the preflight scrub test was tautological. It read capsys after _run_gate had drained it, and checked stderr while errors are emitted as JSON on stdout. Rewrote it against the returned payload and added a negative control that fails when the scrubber is removed.

TDD throughout: 18 new tests written first, 18 confirmed red, then implemented. Suite is 1081 passing with 100 percent coverage on optimize-artifact.py at 474 statements, _optimizer_core.py at 259, and _optimizer_adapters.py at 89.
Re-proved against the real incident pair three ways: pinned, candidate envelope stripped, and split pin deleted. All three REJECT with compared false, consultations 0, and zero ledger files written.

Nothing crashed, since main catches ValueError, but a binary input produced an error document typed UnicodeDecodeError where every other unreadable input says ConfigError.

The recheck emitted _corpus_refusal() | {sel_consultations: spent}, so the key set alone said which read caught the mismatch.

workLog.phase: Round 18: closing five unresolved PR review threads
actions: Two Copilot threads flagged the retracted agent-path claim surviving in generated memory artifacts: the episode file asserted twelve of twenty-four agent fixtures corroborated the rule-path finding and called the agent path live-validated end to end, and the causal graph carried the same sentence as a milestone label. The session log had carried the retraction since the day it was made; the artifacts were stale because every commit this session used SKIP_AUTOFIX=1, and that is exactly the condition under which lefthook skips extract-session-episodes and update-causal-graph.

Tried regeneration first, per the generated-artifacts rule. It cannot fix this: the hook always passes --preserve, so the extractor merges fresh extraction over the existing file and never drops an event whose text is no longer derivable from the source. Proved it by re-running the hook and watching the stale event survive. Checked the alternative: --force rebuilds from the session log and does remove the claim, but it drops events e014 through e017, four real records of the round-16 and round-17 work, and renumbers the rest. Regenerating would have destroyed more truth than it restored.

Corrected the one stale event in place instead, replacing the withdrawn claim with the retraction and its cause: the two runs disagree on fixture_set_sha, so the corpus moved with the prompt and the comparison was confounded rather than a null control. Then re-ran the extractor to prove --preserve carries the correction forward rather than reverting it, and re-ran update-causal-graph, which picked the corrected text up and rewrote the milestone label. Both artifacts now hold zero occurrences of the withdrawn claim.

The significance-bar refusal named two numbers and labeled neither, so a reader could not tell the family bar from the corrected per-comparison bar. The round-14 test asserted only that both numbers appear, which is presence, not legibility. Wrote four tests first covering the labels, the arithmetic, the removed fragment, and the family-of-one edge where the two numbers are equal, confirmed four red, then rewrote the message to name each bar and show the division.

The README corpus example showed a truncated digest ending in an ellipsis, which the reader rejects: _CORPUS_RE requires exactly sixty-four lowercase hex characters. Worse, the invented tail did not even match the real digest's prefix. Replaced it with the actual fixture_set_sha of the incident run, then proved by running the tool that the full value parses while truncated and upper-case values exit 2 as ConfigError, and documented that contract next to the example.

ADR-087 had two lists both numbered to 5 and both referenced as bare Requirement N, so the CodeRabbit thread on Decision Requirement 5 versus Open Requirement 5 was a real ambiguity. The document already used Open Requirement 6 once, so the vocabulary existed and was simply not applied. Defined both labels where each list is introduced and qualified all five remaining bare references after confirming each one's referent by reading it.

Two more threads arrived while the first five were being closed, both on the same claim: every statement of the round-fourteen problem quoted 1 - 0.95**5, about 0.226, as the family-wise false accept probability of five consultations at 0.05. The reviewer is right that this is exact only under independence, and the five comparisons are not independent: all five look at the same selection group, and successive candidates are correlated edits of one artifact. Checked the arithmetic both ways before accepting: the dependence-agnostic union bound is 5 * 0.05 = 0.25, the independence figure is 0.226219.

The conclusion does not move, since both numbers are roughly five times the requested 0.05, so a per-comparison threshold still fails to bound a family and Bonferroni is still right. What was wrong was arguing for a dependence-agnostic correction by citing an independence-only figure, which is reasoning the mechanism itself rejects. Corrected all five live sites, the docstring, the README, the ADR, the test rationale, and the Serena memory, leaving the session log and the round-fourteen debate narrative as the historical record with a correcting note appended.
workLog.outcome: Seven review threads closed, and the two highest-priority were the ones where a claim I had already retracted was still being published by a generator I had been skipping all session. 1102 tests pass with 100 percent coverage on all three optimizer modules; ruff and mypy clean; zero em or en dashes in any changed file. Three lessons generalize. A retraction is not complete when the source document carries it, only when every derived artifact does, and SKIP_AUTOFIX buys commit speed by deferring exactly the generators that keep derived artifacts honest. Asserting that both numbers appear in a refusal does not test that a reader can tell which is which. And a number carried into five documents by copying is corrected in five places or in none, with the test docstring the most likely to be missed, because nobody greps rationale prose when they change a claim.

workLog.phase: Round 18b: the independence assumption, and closing all thirteen threads
actions: Two threads arrived mid-close, both on the same claim. workLog.phase: Round 19: an adversarial review that could not see the disclosures
actions: Ran round 19 on gpt-5.6-terra, a model family used in no previous round, read-only, at extended reasoning. It returned six findings in 411 seconds. Verified each against the code rather than accepting any of them.

The two findings marked Critical are false positives against the stated threat model, and the disclosures are what proved it. The first (the optimizer can read held-out outcomes straight from extract output) is verbatim ADR-087 Open Requirement 1, and README lines 461-469 end with the sentence 'do not cite a run of this loop as evidence against an adversarial optimizer'. The second (EVAL_LEDGER_DIR resets the budget) is Open Requirement 10 and is documented in _ledger_root's own docstring. Neither was fixed: they are the user's deferred decisions, not defects. The lesson recorded in the debate log is that a reviewer reading only code will re-report every deliberately deferred limit as a Critical, because from inside the code a measured hole and an unnoticed one look identical.

Finding 3 fixed TDD. The reviewer had the symptom right and the remedy wrong: they wanted sel_consultations to hold the prior total, but the _corpus_refusal docstring defines consultations as this run's charge and sel_consultations as the running total including it. The real defects were that consultations was absent from both charged sites, so the key answering 'what did this cost me' was missing exactly where the answer is nonzero, and that the ledger-mismatch refusal emitted sel_consultations 0, a number that is never true since the ledger is parsed before the mismatch raises. Wrote 7 tests, confirmed 6 red and 1 passing control, applied the fix, all 7 green. The charged value is derived as spent_after minus spent rather than written as a literal 1 twice, citing this session's own copied-number defect.

Findings 4 and 5 fixed TDD together. Wrote 9 tests, confirmed 6 red and 3 passing controls. _write_atomic's cleanup unlink sat inside except BaseException unguarded, and main catches only ConfigError, AdapterError and ValueError, so an OSError from that unlink escaped as a traceback naming the cleanup instead of the write. It is now suppressed on OSError while every other class still escapes. The rename was also never followed by a parent-directory fsync, so a crash after a reported charge could undo it and hand the consultation back for free, inverting the charge-before-scoring ordering. Added _fsync_dir, called inside the guarded block, skipped on Windows since it cannot open a directory as a descriptor and os.replace is atomic there.

Found one defect the reviewer missed while writing those tests: the handler comment claimed it closed the descriptor when os.fdopen failed, and nothing called os.close, so the path leaked a descriptor while the comment said otherwise. The red test test_a_descriptor_is_closed_when_fdopen_fails proves it. This is the argument for writing the test rather than applying the patch.

Finding 6 fixed in five sites. The earlier correction said Bonferroni 'holds under any dependence'. It controls the family bar under arbitrary dependence among the p-values, but only given each per-comparison p-value is valid on its own, and the exact McNemar tail earns that only if discordant pairs are independent fair coin flips under the null. This harness's own rule-path null control reproduced both gains under a byte-identical no-op, which is direct evidence its outcomes are correlated. Qualified the claim in the gate docstring, the test rationale, the README, ADR-087, and the Serena memory.

Independently verified mcnemar_exact before trusting any p-value it reports: brute-forced all 2**n outcome sequences for every (n, b) pair with n from 0 to 12 against the implementation. Zero mismatches. Concordant pairs correctly excluded, and the docstring's power claims are exact (3 discordant floors at 0.125; n=5 b=5 gives 0.03125; n=7 b=7 gives 0.0078125).

Full verification after all fixes: 1118 tests pass, 100% coverage on all three optimizer files (optimize-artifact.py 494 statements, _optimizer_core.py 259, _optimizer_adapters.py 89), ruff clean, mypy clean, and a byte-level scan showing zero em or en dashes across all seven changed files.

The value is preserved either way, but a tool-driven config migration does not belong in an eval-harness PR, and adopting the rename is the user's call.

workLog.phase: Round 20: a fix that inherited responsibility for where it sat
actions: Ran round 20 on gemini-3.1-pro-preview, a vendor family used in no previous round, read-only, at high reasoning, against the three commits that had had no review at all. It returned three findings in 415 seconds. Verified each empirically before acting, in both directions.

Finding 2 is a false positive and was disproved by running it. The reviewer claimed mcnemar_exact raises OverflowError for n >= 1024 because 2**n exceeds the maximum float. Python's int-by-int true division divides exactly and rounds, so it succeeds whenever the result is representable. Measured directly: n=1023 gives 1.11e-308, n=1024 gives 5.56e-309, n=2000 and n=5000 give 0.0, and n=2000 with b=1100 gives 4.23e-06. A p-value of 0.0 at n=5000 all in one direction is correct to float precision and makes the gate stricter, not looser. No change.

Finding 1 is real and is a defect the previous round created. Defect shape 24 added a parent-directory fsync after os.replace so a crash could not undo a recorded charge. Raising ConfigError when that fsync fails is wrong twice: the message said 'could not write' when the bytes, the mode and the rename had all already succeeded, and more seriously it was the first failure in that function that can fire after the write has landed. In the gate the ledger is written before scoring, so raising there charges a consultation and returns no verdict. Charging before scoring exists so a crash costs the caller a look rather than granting one; aborting after the charge is that same trade pointing the other way. Fixed TDD with four tests plus a control: the loss is now named on stderr, which the exit-code contract keeps free while stdout carries the one JSON document a caller parses, the write stands, and every failure that precedes the rename still refuses.

Finding 3 is real, a Nit by severity and a boundary question by substance. The exhausted-budget refusal advised the operator to 'report on the test group', but score --group has choices=('opt',) and argparse rejects anything else statically. The reviewer offered widening the choice as one remedy. That is the wrong direction: the README lists 'score --group opt refuses to read any other group' among the properties enforced whether or not the optimizer cooperates, and widening it would hand the loop unmetered reads of the group held back as a final unbiased look. Making a message true by weakening the boundary it describes is not a fix. The advice was removed, and the capability it pointed at was filed as issue #3552 for the ADR-087 Open Requirements list.

Recorded defect shapes 26 and 27 in the debate log. Both share this log's recurring root, prose asserting what the mechanism does not do, but the honest repair in each was to change the mechanism's contract rather than its words: shape 26 by deciding what a post-rename failure should cost, shape 27 by deciding that the boundary outranks the sentence describing it.

Full verification: 1127 tests pass, 100% coverage on all three optimizer files (optimize-artifact.py 497 statements, _optimizer_core.py 259, _optimizer_adapters.py 89), ruff clean, mypy clean, zero em or en dashes across every changed file.

workLog.phase: Round 21: a warning held to weaker rules than the raise it replaced
actions: Merged origin/main, which had moved seven commits ahead including another agent's implementation of #3474 and #3475, two issues this session filed. One textual conflict, import-only, resolved as the union of both sides. One semantic conflict git could not see: main's new test_rule_extract_clean_report_succeeds asserts the pre-envelope extract shape, which this branch wraps in a corpus envelope. Git merged both cleanly and the suite failed. Fixed to match the branch convention used at six other sites.

The merge dropped coverage to 99 percent. Main's degraded-report scan arrived with four uncovered lines: a non-object scenario entry, a scenario with no mechanisms block, and a FAIL_JUDGE_ERRORS summary verdict with no scenario already carrying it. The PR body claims 100 percent as its verification, so the merge closes them with three tests rather than shipping a claim the merge had made false.

Ran round 21 on gpt-5.5 at xhigh, read-only, scoped to only the two commits no reviewer had seen, with explicit instructions naming the two failure modes previous rounds hit: re-reporting disclosed ADR limits as Criticals, and asserting runtime behavior without running it. It returned two findings, both Required, both verified by running.

Finding 1: round 20's warning is itself unguarded. print raises when stderr is closed, and _write_atomic converts any OSError from that region into ConfigError, so the abort round 20 removed came back through the diagnostic reporting on its absence. The reviewer demonstrated it with a stderr whose write raises errno 32 rather than arguing it from source.

Finding 2: the warning bypasses _digest_scrubbed, which is a context manager over raised exceptions. A diagnostic that prints and returns never enters it, so a digest-bearing EVAL_LEDGER_DIR root printed unredacted. The seam's own docstring predicted this. The tenth review had already fixed the same leak by hand at the lock-cleanup warning; round 20 added a second site and the hand-fix did not generalize, which is the exact failure a seam exists to prevent.

Fixed both TDD under one seam. _ACTIVE_HOLDOUT_KEY plus a _warn helper that scrubs with the active key and prints under suppressed OSError; _digest_scrubbed publishes the key and restores the previous value in a finally so the seam nests. _warn takes no key parameter on purpose: the caller with no key to pass is the caller who will leak. Both warning sites route through it, which also repairs the older unguarded print at the lock cleanup that had been fixed for leakage only.

Eight tests: five red (closed-stderr crash at both sites, digest leak at both sites, key restore under nesting) and three green controls (a warning with no active key still prints, a raised error still scrubs, the key clears after the scrub exits). 1382 pass, 100 percent on all three optimizer modules, ruff and mypy clean.

Recorded as debate-log defect shape 28: when a failure path is downgraded to a diagnostic, the diagnostic inherits every obligation the failure had. It must not disclose what the raise redacts, and must not fail where the code it reports on succeeded.

workLog.phase: Round 22: guarding the exception a reviewer raised, and a coverage claim no test backed
actions: Ran round 22 on gpt-5.6-sol at xhigh, read-only, scoped to the two commits round 21 produced, with explicit instructions naming the two failure modes prior reviewers hit. It returned three findings. All three were verified independently by running before any code changed.

Finding 1, Required and confirmed twice by measurement. Round 21 gave the post-rename warning back the two properties the raise path had, and guarded it with suppress(OSError) because errno 32 was what the reviewer's demonstration raised. A stream closed for real raises ValueError, not OSError: closing an io.StringIO and warning through it escaped the guard and aborted a write that had already succeeded, which is the exact outcome rounds 20 and 21 both existed to prevent. The worse half is not a crash. sys.stderr is None in an embedded or windowed interpreter and print(file=None) falls back to stdout, the stream carrying the JSON verdict. Measured directly: the warning text landed in captured stdout. A diagnostic that corrupts the payload it is diagnosing is worse than one that crashes, because nothing reports it.

Fixed by stating three named rules in _warn's docstring and holding all three, rather than handling a third case. It snapshots sys.stderr once, returns when there is no stream, and suppresses Exception rather than one subclass. Two rounds each handled the case in front of them and each left the next one open.

Finding 2, Optional and taken. The module global holding the active holdout key was correct for a single-threaded CLI but wrong as a primitive: a second live scope in another context overwrote it and left a stale key behind. Replaced with a ContextVar, set with a token and released with reset(token) rather than set(None), so a nested scrub restores its parent's key instead of clearing it.

Finding 3, Optional and the most serious of the three. Round 21's commit message, phase 16 of this log, and the PR body all claimed the fix was covered 'at both sites' and 'under nesting'. AST inspection and a direct read confirm all eight of those tests drove _write_atomic; none touched the lock-cleanup warning site and none nested a scrub. The code was correct at both sites. The claim about the evidence was not, and it is the one claim a reader cannot check by reading the code.

CORRECTION to phase 16 of this log. Where phase 16 says the round-21 tests cover 'the closed-stderr crash at both sites, the digest leak at both sites, and key restore under nesting', that was untrue when written. Round 21 covered one site and no nesting. This phase adds the two missing tests rather than editing phase 16, because a log that silently repairs its own errors cannot be used as evidence about the process that produced them.

Five tests added, every one mutation-checked, because round 16 caught a vacuous assertion here. Widening the suppression back to OSError, dropping the None guard, routing the lock-cleanup warning through a raw print, replacing reset(token) with set(None), and swapping the ContextVar for a hand-rolled module global each failed exactly one test.

Caught a non-discriminating test of my own before it shipped. The first draft of the context-isolation test used two threads and a barrier and passed against the module global it was written to rule out. Instrumenting the interleaving explained it: the barrier releases both threads but they still run one at a time, and the second finished its finally restore before the first resumed, so each read its own key from a genuinely shared variable by scheduling luck. Rewrote it with copy_context and no threads; it now fails against the global deterministically. A test whose discriminating power depends on scheduling has not been shown to discriminate by passing or failing once.

Audited Windows skip markers on all new tests. Three force a directory fd through _fsync_refuses and were missing @pytest.mark.skipif(os.name == 'nt'); added. The lock-cleanup test fails Path.unlink instead and is cross-platform.

Verified: 15560 pass across the repo suite, 100 percent on all three optimizer modules (optimize-artifact.py 561 statements, _optimizer_core.py 281, _optimizer_adapters.py 89). ruff clean, mypy clean.

Documented as defect shapes 29 (guarding the exception, not the rule) and 30 (a coverage claim no test backed) in the debate log, plus a note on the test that could not fail. README's durability bullet now states the third rule and why the OSError guard was too narrow.

workLog.phase: Round 23, and the bug the docstring found on its own
actions: While writing the three-rule docstring for _warn, the sentence justifying why _scrub sat outside the suppression turned out to be false in both halves. A redaction that raises leaves the message unprinted either way, because the exception skips the print with the message still bound to its unscrubbed value, so excluding it bought no leak protection. What it bought was a _warn that raises from inside _fsync_dir after a rename had already succeeded, which is the abort rounds 20, 21 and 22 were each spent removing, reintroduced by the fix for round 22. Moved the redaction inside the guard, added a test with _scrub monkeypatched to raise, and verified the reverse arrangement fails it.
Ran round 23 on gemini-3.1-pro-preview, read-only, scoped to the two round-22 commits, with the three prior failure modes named including the new one about trusting prose over test bodies.

It confirmed by running: the suppress(Exception) boundary lets KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit through as intended; snapshotting sys.stderr is the right primitive rather than reading it twice; reset(token) is correct under out-of-order exits and generator suspension; LedgerMismatchError does not leak the key through path.parent, which resolves to the ledger root and excludes the digest-bearing filename; and three of the new tests discriminate under its own mutations.
It raised one Optional finding, structurally right and taken: the context-isolation test drove the ContextVar directly, so it tested the standard library rather than this module's scope.

Its proposed repair does not discriminate as written, which measurement showed and reading would not have. Abandoning a generator mid-scope only abandons it while something holds a reference; CPython drops the last one when the helper returns, closes the generator, and runs the very finally the test needs left undone. Measured both variants against both implementations: as proposed, the global mutation passes; holding the reference, it fails.

The review's own mutation was also weaker than it looked. Rebinding the module attribute to None breaks attribute access rather than behavior, so any test touching the variable raises AttributeError rather than failing an assertion. A mutation has to preserve the API and change only the property under test.

Taking the finding surfaced a limitation neither party was looking for. Closing the abandoned generator from outside its context makes reset refuse a foreign token with ValueError, which pytest reports as an unraisable-exception warning. A token has a constraint the module global did not: a scope entered in one context cannot be exited in another. Every scope in this CLI is a plain with in straight-line synchronous code, so _digest_scrubbed discloses it beside the non-LIFO limitation rather than guarding a path no call site can reach. The test closes its generator inside the context that opened it.
Verified: 1388 pass across the optimizer suites, 100 percent on all three modules, no warnings, ruff clean, mypy clean.
Documented as defect shapes 31 (the docstring found the bug the reviewer did not) and 32 (a proposed fix is a claim like any other) in the debate log.

workLog.phase: Round 24: the last expression nobody guarded
actions: Sent round 24 to the idle round-23 reviewer via write_agent rather than starting a fresh agent, reporting the outcome of its previous finding first: the finding was taken, its proposed patch was measured and rejected because CPython refcount-collects the abandoned generator and runs the finally the test needed left undone, and its proposed mutation broke attribute access rather than behavior. Scoped it read-only to 437923b10 and a541a88cd, named the three recurring reviewer failure modes, and said plainly that a clean verdict would be read as signal rather than as a failure to find something.

It returned a clean verdict on both commits and answered all three questions asked: _warn holds its three rules, _digest_scrubbed's finally restores correctly on every synchronous path, and the copy_context test does discriminate, which it confirmed by building its own API-preserving module global and watching the test fail against it. It then filed one Nit.

The Nit was real and under-labelled. sys.stderr is an attribute lookup, and stream = sys.stderr sat outside the suppression guard, so a harness that deletes the attribute rather than blanking it raises AttributeError from the line whose only job is to decide whether the guard runs. That abort lands after the rename it reports on has already succeeded, which is the same regression class rounds 20 through 23 each closed at a different site.

Reproduced it before believing it, as a red test: monkeypatch.delattr(sys, 'stderr') through _fsync_refuses into _write_atomic gives AttributeError: module 'sys' has no attribute 'stderr' at line 791, with the ledger already renamed.

Fixed with getattr(sys, 'stderr', None), which adds no control flow: the missing attribute routes into the None branch that already existed and was already tested, so one expression becomes total and no second branch is introduced. This is why it was taken rather than filed under the rule against error handling for unreachable paths; it is the difference between a partial and a total read of a value the function already branches on, not a new guard.

Corrected the docstring in the same change. It claimed only the stream check sat outside the guard while the stream read sat outside it too, making the sentence false for the second time in two rounds by the same mechanism as shape 31.

Verified: mutation M7 restores the partial read and fails exactly one test of 380 in the CLI file. 1389 pass across the optimizer suites, up one from the new test. Coverage stays 100% on all three modules and the statement count of optimize-artifact.py does not move, because the change replaced an expression rather than adding a line. Ruff and mypy clean.

Independently re-verified the two prior mutations at HEAD before this change: M5 (ContextVar swapped for an API-preserving module global) fails exactly one test with the cross-context overwrite it exists to catch, and M6 (redaction moved back outside the guard) fails exactly one different test with the redactor's RuntimeError escaping to the caller. Source restored byte-identical after each.

Committed as a33c5c089. Documented as defect shape 33, which is narrower than the four rounds before it: each of those moved a statement into the guard, while this one is about an expression that was never a candidate for moving because it reads as a fetch rather than as work.

Amended the operator doc's durability bullet, which said sys.stderr can be absent and described only the blanked case. Absent covers two cases and the deleted one raises from the read rather than redirecting the write, so the bullet now names both.

workLog.phase: Two review threads, one real defect, and the test that already knew
actions: The Copilot PR reviewer left two unresolved threads, both naming the same mismatch: ADR-087 requirement 5 and the Serena memory each said the gate refuses unless the split's pin and both results files name one corpus, while the same sections went on to describe an all-unknown case that is reported rather than refused.

Verified against _corpus_conflict rather than against the prose. The rule is that the declared corpora, with absent ones dropped, must not exceed one distinct value. All unknown collapses to a single value and is not a conflict; a known corpus beside an unknown one is two values and is. The reviewer was right on both counts and the docs overstated the rule.

The behaviour already had a test. The parametrised truth table pins (UNPINNED, None, None) to False, so the code was correct and only the prose drifted. No test was added, because adding one would duplicate a case already covered rather than close a gap.

Corrected both documents to state the rule the code enforces, and said in the ADR that the earlier wording read as refusing the all-unknown case. This is the same defect class the log calls shape 25, a claim stated more strongly than it holds, arriving this time from a bot reviewer rather than from the author.

Merged origin/main, which had moved four commits and reported CONFLICTING on the generated causal graph. Resolved by regenerating rather than by hand; the regenerated file matched the merge result exactly, so the merge was already correct. 1389 pass after the merge, ruff clean.

Grepped for the old wording rather than trusting the two threads to be exhaustive, and found a third copy of the same overstatement in the operator README that neither thread named. Corrected it in the same shape. A bot reviewer reports what it read, not what it did not read, so a finding about prose is a reason to search for the prose elsewhere.

Then found a precision bug in that fix. The README correction said a declared corpus beside an undeclared one is a disagreement, and undeclared reads as the absent split key, which is exactly the case that is NOT a conflict. The ADR survived the same wording only because a neighbouring paragraph disambiguates it; the README had no such neighbour. Rewrote it to name the two absences separately: a results file says null, which counts as a value, while a split with no corpus key names nothing and is dropped before counting. Verified all six resulting claims against _corpus_conflict directly, zero mismatches.
Replied to both threads with the fix, the reason no test was added, and the third copy neither thread named. Resolved both.

workLog.phase: Round twenty-five: the first clean verdict, and the finding inside it
actions: Round twenty-five (gpt-5.6-luna) answered all five questions with method labels and probe evidence, and found nothing in the code. That reading survives; the code is correct.

It reported that the key read is also lexically outside the guard, then set it aside as shorthand rather than a defect because the read cannot raise. The premise is right and the conclusion is not: the docstring said only one read sat outside the guard and two do.

Measured the risk instead of asserting it. Removing default=None from the ContextVar turns thirteen tests red, so the invariant is pinned, but every one of the thirteen is about stderr or scrubbing and none names the constructor argument that caused it.

Fixed a stale sentence the change created in a neighbouring test docstring, which quoted the sentence being replaced.

workLog.phase: Three bot threads, one accepted whole and two accepted for a different reason
actions: The memory doc said three load-bearing details and listed eight. Counted the items rather than trusting either number, found exactly eight, and corrected the header. The cause was a drifted edit: the list grew one entry per review round and the header never moved.

Rejected the stated reason for the two banned-word threads. `significant` is banned because it substitutes a vague adjective for a number; statistical significance carries one. Left `significance bar` where it names the feature and left `test_a_regression_is_not_significant` alone, since a one-sided test for improvement really does return p of 1.0 for a regression.

Accepted the rename for a different reason the threads did not give. `gate(0.8, 0.6, p_value=0.25)` is a twenty-point gain called insignificant, which inverts the finding: the effect is large and only the evidence is weak. Renamed to name the tail.

actions: Sent round twenty-six (gpt-5.6-terra) at the correction itself rather than the code, on the grounds that the docstring had been false in three consecutive rounds, each time right after someone corrected it.

It was right that 'two reads sit outside the guard' is false as a literal count, since the suppress and Exception lookups and __enter__ are out there too, and right that the declaration sits sixty lines above the read rather than fifty.

1390 pass, 100% on the CLI module held, ruff and mypy clean. Committed cdd704367.

actions: Four rounds corrected this docstring and four corrections were falsified, two of them by the commit that corrected the previous one. Treated that rate as evidence about the paragraph rather than about the readers.

workLog.phase: Making the corpus refusal name only what every refusing input carries
actions: A bot reviewer objected that the refusal advises re-scoring against the corpus the split was drawn from, while a --tasks split pins no corpus. Reproduced the refusing row directly: _corpus_conflict(_UNPINNED, SHA_A, SHA_B) is True, so a pinless split does reach that message.

workLog.phase: Pinning the payload presence rule for the two keys it was never written for
actions: Round twenty-seven (gemini-3.1-pro-preview) was aimed at the decision logic rather than the diagnostic helper the previous rounds had circled. It cleared every ACCEPT and REFUSE path: strict slice boundaries make overlap structurally impossible, ties refuse, the Bonferroni family size is the declared cap, adapters raise on duplicate ids, and errored tasks record as failures instead of shrinking the denominator.

Its one finding was that REJECT has three payload shapes. Verified by an AST pass over every emit site: pre-lock refusals carry four keys, ledger mismatch six, guard and coverage seven, a verdict sixteen. The observation is true.

Rejected the proposed remedy on evidence rather than argument. Querying the ledger so the preflight could report sel_consultations reverses round seventeen, which removed that key so a key set alone could not reveal which of the two corpus reads caught the disagreement, and it would read the ledger before the lock.

Measured the other half. Applied the fix to the drift refusal and ran the suite: the payload then reports a fingerprint of all zeroes beside a reason saying that fingerprint does not describe the file. The drift check is what disproved the value, so that site cannot state it honestly.

Found the real defect inside the rejected fix. The README stated the presence rule for consultations and sel_consultations and was silent on group and fingerprint, and no test pinned them, so a careful reader given the payloads and no rule reaches exactly the conclusion this round reached.

Added TestWhichRefusalsNameTheGroupTheyOpened, five tests covering the verdict, an under-lock refusal, the drift refusal, the no-echo-of-a-disproved-fingerprint edge, and the corpus refusal from both sides of the lock.

Confirmed the class earns its place by mutation. M10 applies round twenty-seven's fix to the drift refusal: before this commit nothing broke, after it two tests fail, and the failure output is the self-contradicting payload itself.

Extended the README accounting-keys paragraph to cover all four keys, naming the corpus refusal as the one deliberate exception and the reason it is one: a single document emitted from both sides of the lock carries only what the earlier side can say.
Recorded shape 37 in the debate log: a contract documented for some of the keys it governs reads as an accident at the keys it skipped.
Verified 1396 pass, 100 percent statement coverage held on all three eval modules, ruff and mypy clean, zero em or en dashes byte-verified across every edited file.

Triaged a bot thread on ADR-087 claiming the Bonferroni caveat was missing a subject. The claim is false: the subject is 'looks', a plural noun repeated from earlier in the same sentence, so 'which looks at one selection group are not' parses. The complaint is right for a reason the bot did not give, which is that 'looks' sits immediately after 'which', where English prefers a verb reading, so the reader garden-paths and reparses at 'are not'.

Fixed it by making the ADR match the README, which already states the same caveat with an explicit plural subject ('and five looks at one selection group are not') rather than by inventing new prose. Word diff confirms the only semantic change is one clause becoming a sentence; everything else is rewrap. No decision, requirement, consequence, or status changed, so this is a copy edit rather than an ADR revision and adr-review was not fired.

workLog.phase: Making score refuse the drifted split it was quietly vouching for
actions: Asked round twenty-seven the generalisation of its own finding: does any other emitted field carry a value some site cannot state honestly, and is there a fifth field varying under no rule and no test. Told it to enumerate the emit sites by reading them and that a negative answer with the work shown would beat another finding.

It found one and ran it. cmd_score prints split['fingerprint'] beside the score and never checks whether the fingerprint still describes the file. cmd_gate checks on the line after its read; _split_drifted has one caller and _read_split has two.

Reproduced independently on a real split rather than the fabricated one it used. Drew a split, dropped one opt task, left the fingerprint, and scored twice: same fingerprint, n of 6 then 5, score 0.333 then 0.200. An operator whose path was wrong was told to wait for a process that does not exist or clear a lock never taken, and the message that would name the real cause is the one the other branch prints. M46, M47, M48 each took 2 red. M49 reversed the walk and survived. workLog.phase: Phase forty-one: the rule path stops asking one judge once
actions: Resolved the open end-to-end question by reading ADR-087 Open Requirement 5 rather than running anything: a live rule-path validation ran 2026-07-27 via GitHub Models. It produced a false accept, and the null control caught it. A negative demonstration is a demonstration, and it is the more informative direction.

That run is what promoted Open Requirement 6 from a suspicion to a measurement. Scoring identical rule text twice moved 13 of 24 tasks and 5 across the pass threshold, mean absolute movement 0.49 points on a five-point judge scale. The two held-out gains behind the false accept were the two largest movements in that benchmark.

Read the producer before designing the consumer. eval-rule-activation.py has no runs flag and writes one scores block per mechanism, so an in-record runs list would have been a consumer for data nobody makes. The ADR's own paired measurement was gathered by invoking the producer twice, so the run unit is a whole report and no producer change is needed.
TDD: 16 tests written and run red (ImportError on rule_results_multi), then green. Eval suite 1627 to 1643.
Extracted _rule_run_scores so both entry points share one implementation rather than sniffing the input shape, which is the missing-model smell the review skill names.
decisions: Reduce over scores, not over verdicts. Thresholding each run and voting discards the distance from the bar, which is the only thing that says whether a disagreement was close. This also matches agent_results, so the two noisy adapters now read the same way.

A scenario with evidence in some runs but not others is refused, not scored False and not silently dropped. False is actively unsafe in the incumbent direction: a judge error on the incumbent's run reads as a failing scenario, so a candidate that merely ran cleanly looks like a fail-to-pass improvement. That is the spurious accept the gate exists to prevent, arriving through the scorer. Dropping the run reduces over a different sample size per scenario without saying so.
Uniform absence stays False, which is what makes rule_results_multi([s]) == rule_results(s) hold exactly. That equality is a test, not a claim.

#3445 was on the deferred-to-owner list and was taken off it. Open Requirement 3 (#3437, the boolean seam) is marked in the ADR as the user's call; Open Requirement 6 carries a directive Proposed section instead. The marker is the difference, not the issue number.

workLog.phase: Phase forty-two: round thirty-nine, and a refusal that leaked around itself
actions: Ran round 39 as a code-review agent on gpt-5.6-sol at xhigh, scoped to the four commits since round 38, with instructions to reproduce before reporting. It returned three Critical findings and nothing else. All three reproduced independently before any test was written.

F6: os.dup2 needs a descriptor, so a stand-in stream left the broken stdout installed and CPython's shutdown flush replaced the status with 120 after the function returned 2. Measured before at exit 120 with 'Exception ignored'; after, exit 2 clean. A unit test cannot catch this, because pytest restores stdout before interpreter shutdown, so the test is a subprocess.

TDD: 7 tests written and confirmed red for the right reasons, then green. Eval suite 1689 to 1695. One of the 7 was wrong before the code was, the fourth bad instrument this session: it stood in a closed io.StringIO for a closed stdout, and a closed StringIO's flush returns quietly.

Reclassified by content, with the filter refusing rather than guessing on any hunk it could not place, and verified the intermediate commit green at 590 tests before committing.

decisions: The F5 fix adds an answer rather than widening a guard. _corpus_conflict's anti-strip rule is real and something has to hold it, so tolerating an unreadable file there would buy the malformed case by selling the stripped one. A negative control test that was green before the fix and stayed green after is what holds that line.

Gave the sentinel a class instead of a bare object(). _UNREADABLE = object() made the return type str | object | None, which collapses to object and checks nothing. As a one-line class the type became str | _Unreadable | None and mypy immediately failed the call site, because the sentinel flows into _corpus_conflict, which is written against str | None. The bare-object version would have shipped that hole silently.

_detach_stdout still prefers the devnull redirect and falls back to sys.stdout = None, rather than assigning None directly. The redirect keeps a real stream in place for anything that writes afterward. It also closes the descriptor it opens, because os.dup2 duplicates it and leaking one per exit is wrong to write down as intentional.

ADR-087 Open Requirement 6 is recorded as still open, not as landed. A mechanism exists, but nothing enforces a run count and the replication rate is still unmeasured, which is what the requirement actually asked for.

workLog.phase: Phase forty-three: two push gates that cannot both be satisfied by a linear history
actions: Removed all three type suppressions rather than justifying them, because the push gate has no allowance to justify one in place. The type: ignore[index] existed because the rule dispatch built a parallel list of booleans, checked all(), then re-indexed the payloads behind that check; collecting the values in the first pass removed both the suppression and the second traversal. Used len(envelopes) == len(payloads) rather than a truth test so an empty input keeps taking the envelope path the way all([]) did.

Probed the alternative to the two type: ignore[assignment] on sys.stdout and found the whole file-descriptor path unnecessary. sys.stdout = io.StringIO() handles the stream whose fileno raises and the real broken pipe identically to an os.dup2 devnull redirect, needs no descriptor to open or guard or close, and cannot fail at construction. Deleted _detach_stdout; its three branches collapsed to one assignment.

Hit the structural wall: every intermediate commit added a suppression and only the tip removed them, so no partial push was clean either, while the full 45-commit stack exceeded the ceiling. Rewrote the unpushed history into three layered commits after tagging pre-squash-backup, and verified the adapter-only intermediate green at 1648 before committing it.
Verified the rewrite lost nothing: git diff --quiet pre-squash-backup HEAD reports an identical tree, and the suite is 1695 on both.
decisions: Eliminate the suppressions idiomatically rather than seek a bypass. The gate is right that a suppression is a smell, and in all three cases the code that needed one was the worse code: two traversals where one would do, and a descriptor dance where an object swap suffices.

Rewrite history rather than push in stages. Two gates bind at once. _check_commit_limit counts the whole three-branch stack from main against 40 and its only relief is a label on an open PR, which cannot exist before the first push. _added_suppression_violations refuses any commit in the pushed range that adds a suppression and has no relief at all. Rewriting is safe here only because nothing was pushed.

Group by layer rather than by finding. The twelve original commits told the review story, but that story belongs in the PR body, which survives a squash. The three that remain are separable: the adapter layer is green without the CLI, so an intermediate is a real state rather than a bisect trap.

Measured whether a validator could catch dead hashes before proposing one. Over the session log and the debate log, a hex token rule found forty six candidates, thirty five resolving to commits and eleven not. All eleven were false positives: a p-value of 0.0078125, the interior of the word succeeded, dates and random suffixes from run directory names, and truncated corpus fingerprints. True positives: zero.
decisions: Do not build the dead-hash validator. Its only finding bucket was one hundred percent false positives on the first run, and a gate that opens that way gets an ignore list and then a skip flag. Prose does not record intent, so a detector over prose can only match shape, and hex is a shape that dates, probabilities, digests and ordinary English words share.
Cite pull request numbers rather than commit hashes in anything that outlives a branch. A number survives every rewrite and cannot be confused with a p-value.

workLog.phase: Third main merge into the buffer-crash branch, and recording shape 66
actions: Re-merged origin/main into fix/eval-buffer-crash-exit-code for the third time this session. Main advanced by two commits (304355e98 closing stale execution plans, 03569ca57 resolving module wiring for issue #3360) after the previous merge, which flipped PR #3579 back to CONFLICTING. Reset the worktree to the remote branch first so the merge ran against what GitHub sees, merged clean with no conflicted paths, confirmed 1697 passed and that the branch still owns zero plugin paths, and pushed as 1ebc1fb3d.

Recorded shape 66 in the ADR-087 debate document. The round-45 F4 finding was real and measured, but the justification the plan carried for the fix was invented: it claimed the split fingerprint is computed over the JSON string, so exact-string comparison was the right bar. Reading split_fingerprint disproved that. It calls _canonical_ratio, which runs the value through Fraction, so 0.4, '0.4' and '0.40' all hash to fa2b51a4f24c8cb2 and only the long-decimal respelling differs. An exact-string bar would have failed on '0.40', a respelling the product cannot distinguish anywhere it matters, so the planned fix would have shipped a false-positive test.

The general form is the ninth instrument failure this session: a finding can be true while the reason attached to it is invented, because reasoning about a function that has not been opened produces prose of the same confidence as reasoning about one that has. The discipline is to read the cited function before the justification is written into a commit message, since a wrong reason does not stay inert, it selects the wrong fix.
workLog.outcome: PR #3579 re-merged with main and pushed as 1ebc1fb3d with 1697 passing. The disproved-justification episode is recorded as shape 66 so the next round treats a plan's stated rationale as a claim to verify, not a premise.

workLog.phase: Round 46: four review findings, and replacing the window rule with the repo's parser
actions: Reproduced all four findings from the gpt-5.6-sol review before accepting any of them. The bool hole is real: _defaults_agree routed a bool to the direct-comparison branch, where bool subclasses int and False == 0.0 is True, so a ratio flag rewritten as store_true read as unchanged while _canonical_ratio(False) raises 'must be a decimal ratio'. The bar approved what the product refuses. Fixed by making a mixed bool/number pair a mismatch, with two bools still comparing as bools so a future store_true flag keeps working. Mutation-verified both directions with --test-ratio defaulted to False.

The three window findings were also real and shared one cause: the block-start rule was hand-written, so it missed every construct its own list did not name. Measured five: prose on the line after a fence closes stayed inside the fence, an indented run of backticks opened a fence that swallowed the heading below it, a thematic break did not end a block, a setext underline did not, and a blockquote written without its space did not. Patching each is a pattern per construct with the next construct always outstanding.

Replaced the state machine with markdown-it-py, which this repo already depends on and already reads Markdown with through scripts/utils/markdown_parser. _markdown_block now takes the narrowest token map covering the marker's line, skipping inline content tokens so the window is the block the renderer drew rather than what it drew inside. That deleted two regexes and thirty lines of fence and heading bookkeeping, and put the dialect in one place instead of two.

Two of the reported cases turned out to be correct already and were left alone: a tilde fence is not closed by a backtick line, so an unclosed fence running to end of document is the right answer, and four-space-indented backticks are paragraph continuation rather than a fence. Two of my own written expectations were wrong instead of the code, both about CommonMark rather than about this helper: a setext underline makes a heading of every line above it, and a dash run under a paragraph underlines it while the same run after a blank line divides. Both are now pinned as tests in their own right.

Evidence: all four live README windows are byte-identical before and after at 12, 7, 5 and 5 lines, so no existing assertion changed meaning. Nine new cases fail when the old helper is spliced back in. On the real README, injecting a thematic break plus a contradicting exit-code sentence leaves the old window returning seven lines including the contradiction and the new window returning the marker line alone. Suite 1849 passed.

Importing the parser surfaced two pre-existing mypy errors in scripts/utils/markdown_parser.py, where parse_sections indexed a token map straight after a None check that narrowing cannot survive across a list element. Bound both to locals, which keeps the guard and makes it legible, rather than suppressing. Committed separately from the change that depends on it.
workLog.outcome: Three atomic commits on feat/eval-rule-multirun: 1c17fbd97 the bool bar, 45070a105 the parser module narrowing, 652555541 the parser-derived window. Suite 1849 passed with ruff and mypy clean on both changed files, and the reviewer has the new implementation to attack.

workLog.phase: Round 47: recovering five commits GitHub deleted under me, and two more review findings
actions: PR #3608 was squash-merged into its base while my push was in flight. GitHub deleted the head branch on merge, so the push that had already cleared every local hook was rejected with 'cannot lock ref: unable to resolve reference', and the retry failed differently: the commit-limit bypass resolves through an open PR, and there was no longer one. Five commits carrying the whole round-46 fix set existed only on this machine. Confirmed absent from the merged base by ancestry check, then cherry-picked all five onto it. Zero conflicts, suite 1851 passed, byte-identical to what was lost.

The lesson is about ordering, not about git. A push that clears local hooks has not landed; the remote can move underneath it. Verify with ancestry against the remote ref, not with the exit code of the push.

Round 46's review returned two findings and both reproduced. The first says the bool guard I added last round was one instance of a wider hole rather than the hole itself: == compares numbers by value, so an int owner default and a float command default read as agreement. Grounded it in the product rather than in taste: edit_budget is annotated max_edits: int -> int and answers 5.0 when handed one, which json.dumps writes as 5.0 where the published results carried 5. Replaced the bool special case with one rule about kinds, which subsumes it. Seven of the nine live table entries compare same-kind numbers and still pass; the two ratios keep their float-versus-string branch.

The second finding is the same borrowed-neighbour failure the parser was brought in to end, in the one construct the parser cannot decompose. CommonMark ends a raw HTML block at a blank line rather than at the end of an element, so '
a
' followed by '

b

' is one html_block token and the window returned both lines. Separating them needs an HTML parser. The window now refuses a marker inside markup and names the remedy.

Chose the stricter half deliberately and pinned it: a <details> element spanning four lines would be a correct window, but it is the same token type, so accepting it means accepting the borrowing case. Borrowing is silent and a refusal is loud, so the refusal wins. Verified the eval README contains zero html_block tokens and all four of its live windows are byte-identical at 12, 7, 5 and 5 lines.
decisions: Reapplied the lost commits onto the merged base rather than reopening the merged PR. The base branch is the head of open PR #3579, so the work has an open PR to travel on and needs no new one.

Replaced the bool guard rather than adding a second numeric guard beside it. A list of type pairs fails the same way the list of block-start patterns did: it misses whatever it does not name. One rule about kinds is the same move that ended the window findings.

Refused raw HTML rather than returning the token. The window exists so an assertion cannot pass on a neighbour's words; returning a token that may hold two rendered elements gives that guarantee back up silently.
workLog.validation: Suite 1861 passed after both fixes, up from 1851 with ten new cases. Red phase confirmed five of them fail against the previous implementation. ruff clean, mypy clean on the changed file, zero em or en dashes. Real README windows unchanged at 12, 7, 5, 5 lines.

workLog.phase: Round 48: two PRs shipped the same issue, and an outside review of the result
actions: origin/main advanced and conflicted for the first time. The conflicting commit is b61cd3f7b (PR #3573), which also says 'Fixes #3445'. Two independent implementations of ADR-087 Open Requirement 6 landed in the same week. Read every conflict hunk before choosing, and they turn out to attack different axes: #3573 reduces across judge samples inside one run (score_samples, --judge-repeats), mine reduces across whole runs (rule_results_multi, separate report files). Sample repetition drops one erratic judge call. Run repetition catches a whole report landing on the far side of the bar, which is what OR6 actually measured: 13 of 24 tasks moved and 5 crossed the threshold. Neither subsumes the other, so the resolution is a union, not a winner.

Resolved seven conflict regions with a marker-region resolver rather than by hand: a regex over the diff3 shape with an indexed replacement list, asserting the region count and then asserting no markers survive. Where the two designs disagreed the stricter reading won, and each disagreement is observationally identical through the public API: a failed judge sample sets None (no evidence) not False (failure), which rule_results renders False either way; a sample missing a score key raises instead of defaulting to 0, which main already did on its own sampled path. Main's calls also passed two arguments to this branch's bounded _as_float and would have raised TypeError, which the resolution had to fix.

The evidence that the union preserves #3573's contract is that #3573's own suites pass unedited: 1867 passed, 1 pre-existing environmental skip. Editing another author's tests to make a merge green would have destroyed exactly the grounding that makes the claim worth anything. A merge has no natural red phase, so the 8 new union tests were proved by mutation instead: forcing the sample reducer fails 2, reading a failed sample as False fails 1, ignoring score_samples fails 5.

The merge opened a hole in the flag audit. --rule-reduce has argparse dest rule_reduce but its owner parameter is reduce_samples, and the audit table keyed on dest alone would have left it silently unaudited. Two flags now reach rule_results_multi and neither can be named reduce on both sides. Widened _OWNED_DEFAULTS to 4-tuples carrying the owner's parameter name, and mutation-proved it: hardcoding the default fails the new case.

Round 48 review (gemini-3.1-pro-preview, code-review agent, no prior context, 1658s) returned four findings. Three real, one fabricated, holding the roughly five-in-six rate. F3 claimed Ratio is a union including int; it is 'float | str' at _optimizer_core.py:85, and their suggested fix would have regressed round-46 finding #1 by making _defaults_agree(5, 5.0) true again. F4 was real: _corpus_header caught only ValueError and RecursionError, so a mistyped --incumbent escaped as OSError and the envelope reported a raw errno while every other reader says 'no such file: <path>'. Fixed by catching OSError and deferring to the authoritative read, which _corpus_refused already makes safe. F1 was real and the more interesting one: the patch shape guard's placement inside patch_fingerprint was argued in a comment and verified nowhere. Removing it left 448 tests green while the buffer commands lost their refusal, so the six new tests call patch_fingerprint directly, which is the only spelling that can tell the two placements apart.
decisions: Union rather than pick a side. Both reductions are real and complementary, and losing either would have cost a capability the other cannot provide.
Whether both surfaces should survive long term, and which the README and ADR should call canonical, is an architecture call for @rjmurillo. Flagged, not folded in.

The directory case keeps its errno text. _read_text prefixes it with 'could not read <path>' so the file is named first, and for unusual OS failures the detail is the only thing that says what went wrong. The guarantee tested is that the peek stops being the layer that answers, not that errno text disappears.

workLog.phase: Round 49, and losing the branch it was written on
actions: Ran round 49 on gpt-5.6-sol at xhigh with no prior context. Two Required findings, both real. That is the first round in this series where every reported finding survived reproduction; roughly five of six earlier rounds carried at least one confident claim that did not.

Finding 1 invalidated my own round-48 fix. I had made the corpus header peek answer _UNREADABLE for a file it could not open, arguing that _corpus_refused declines to decide so the authoritative read below would still raise ConfigError and exit 2. I traced _corpus_refused but not what runs between the peek and that read. _gate_entry runs the peek, then _corpus_refused, then takes the ledger lock, then runs _guard, and only then reads. _guard emits REJECT when the consultation budget is spent, so with the budget exhausted a mistyped --incumbent produced REJECT at exit 1 instead of a config error at exit 2. Reproduced end to end through the real CLI with no monkeypatching.

The replacement is smaller than what it replaces. _corpus_header now reads through _read_text, which already converts OSError into the canonical ConfigError. ConfigError subclasses Exception rather than ValueError, so it travels past the peek's own decode clause to the top level and exits 2. That fixes the original errno leak and preserves config-error precedence with no OSError clause at all. Reverting it fails 5 tests including the new budget-precedence regression.

Finding 2 showed the owned-defaults audit proves declaration, not forwarding. It asserts a flag's argparse default equals its owner's parameter default, which says nothing about whether the parsed value arrives. The reviewer replaced rule_results_multi with a wrapper that accepted reduce_samples and discarded it, and all 1355 tests in the primary suites stayed green.

Closing finding 2 by mutation surfaced a third forwarding site the review had not named. extract --kind rule forwards --rule-reduce from the flat scenario list read from one --input, the same list read from several, and the multi-rule envelope that produces <rule>::<id> ids. After pinning the first two, hardcoding the envelope's reducer still left all 731 CLI tests passing. Each site now has its own assertion, built so median and mean land on opposite sides of the bar. Mutation fails 1 test at the envelope and 2 at the shared flat site.

The push was rejected after the gate had already run 16360 tests: a collaborator had merged main into the shared branch and pushed a conflict resolution. Merged their tip rather than rebasing, took main's deletion of the causal graph JSON under ADR-089, and re-proved all three mutations on the merged tree rather than trusting the merge.

That merge was blocked by the ADR review gate, which exempts an ADR only when a MERGE_HEAD parent is an ancestor of origin/main. Merging a shared branch tip that already contains main leaves the branch as the parent, so all three ADR paths main contributed read as branch-authored. Confirmed by blob hash that all three were byte-identical to origin/main, then fixed the gate to compare content against origin/main alongside the approved parents. Written test-first; exempting every path during a merge fails 3 tests including the new negative control.

PR #3579 then merged and deleted the branch while this work was still local, so none of it landed. Cherry-picked the three content commits onto a fresh branch off main, verified 1905 eval tests pass there, and opened issue #3658 and a new pull request. The ADR gate fix is no longer blocking on a branch with no merge, so it goes out separately rather than riding along.

Verified the README section empirically rather than asserting it: the example command exits 0, both flags accept all four reducers, the documented defaults match the constants in _optimizer_adapters.py, and a report carrying no score_samples is byte-identical under all four --rule-reduce values.
decisions: Merge the collaborator's tip rather than rebase. The branch was shared the moment someone else pushed to it, and rebasing would have discarded a conflict resolution I did not write and could not reconstruct.

Fix the ADR review gate rather than add review evidence for ADRs I never opened. The alternative was to write adr-review evidence into today's session log for ADR-089, which would have been fabricated evidence in a governance artifact.

Ship the ADR gate fix as its own change rather than folded into the eval work. It blocked a commit, which is why it was written then, but it is an unrelated concern and the new branch does not need it to build.
Split the round-49 work into three commits rather than one. The fix, the forwarding tests, and the documentation each stand on their own evidence and each can be reverted without the others.
